clue.text: Supports – or declines to intervene?

blocks.note: to remain loyal to someone, as a friend in trouble
to look on without acting while something happens

explanation.walkthrough: The same phrasal verb means both loyalty and passivity, which is why the dash and question mark set them against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain phrasal verb with two opposite-feeling senses: staying loyal to a friend, and idly watching events.

clue.text: Break away from some predecessors, being revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters prED ECES sors

explanation.surface: A radical generation breaks with those who came before it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the reversed letters read upwards. 'Revolutionary' seems to describe the rebels; it is the instruction to turn the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a state or member that formally withdraws from a union breaks away from it.

clue.text: One coin per person

blocks.note: a = one, the indefinite article
as in a ten-pence or fifty-cent coin

explanation.surface: A price list: one coin each.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a price, so 'one coin' looks like a single amount rather than two separate chunks: A + PIECE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: charging five pounds to each person is charging that much for every individual.

clue.text: Sam and Everyman cover up problems

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters come out reversed

blocks.note: taken as it stands
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as ME
a lid is a cover

explanation.surface: Two people team up to hush up some trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover up' reads as concealment, but 'cover' is LID and 'up' turns the whole string SAM+ME+LID upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dilemma is a hard choice, a type of problem.

clue.text: Report by young fellow: is he perhaps from S. Asia?

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters might be something else, so 'is he' may be rearranged into another order

blocks.note: a report is a loud noise, as of a gun
a lad is a young fellow
the letters of IS HE rearranged

explanation.surface: A news report asks whether a young man comes from South Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a news item; here it is the noise of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the country sits on the Bay of Bengal in South Asia, so its people are from there.

clue.text: Gives a place to grad – MIT spellbound (to some extent)

indicators.note: 'to some extent' means partly, so only part of the phrase is used

blocks.note: grAD MIT Spellbound

explanation.surface: A graduate is dazzled by the university that has offered them a place.
explanation.walkthrough: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology; the university theme hides that the answer is simply sitting across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the university sense: accepting an applicant is giving them a place on a course.

clue.text: What the Coen Brothers do is straightforward

definitions.note: the first definition is a description of an action, standing for the verb DIRECT

blocks.note: Joel and Ethan Coen make films such as Fargo; think of their job
frank, going straight to the point

explanation.surface: A remark that the Coen Brothers' work is plain and simple.
explanation.walkthrough: The Coen Brothers are American film-makers (Fargo, No Country for Old Men), so what they do is direct.
explanation.definitionFit: Film-makers' job is to run the shoot, and a frank person or a route with no detours is also this.

clue.text: Accounts consisting of utterances

blocks.note: in = made of, as in 'a sculpture in bronze'
voices = spoken expressions

explanation.surface: A description of records made up of spoken words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accounts' suggests stories or reports; here it is the commercial sense, bills.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the commercial sense: an account sent to a customer is a bill for payment.

clue.text: Unwisely realigns with US author

indicators.note: something done unwisely is done badly, so the letters come out in a wrong order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly takes sides with an American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: J. D. Salinger wrote The Catcher in the Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the writer of The Catcher in the Rye was American.

clue.text: 'Relaxing'? Terrifying!

blocks.note: the quotation marks flag a slang word for taking it easy
what makes the blood run cold

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks flag 'relaxing' as slang: chilling out. The two senses are nearly opposite, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for lounging about, and the ordinary sense of making the blood run cold.

clue.text: Weighty and large stones

blocks.note: grave = weighty, serious
L = large, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: Big heavy stones.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as boulders; 'weighty' means serious here, not heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, collective: a path's loose covering of small stones.

clue.text: African shivering with cold; time: 10.35?

indicators.note: shivering shakes things, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: part of the fodder
part of the fodder
part of the fodder, not T this time

explanation.surface: Someone from Africa shivers in the cold, noting the time, 10.35.
explanation.walkthrough: 10.35 looks like a time of day, which the word 'time' encourages; it is a number with a point in it. The question mark flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a number written with a point, where .35 means thirty-five hundredths.

clue.text: Urchins having sport, largely, in itinerant funfairs

indicators.note: 'largely' means for the most part, so only the larger part of the word is kept and its last letter goes
the shortened word goes inside the rearranged letters
an itinerant wanders, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: the letters of FUNFAIRS rearranged; GAM goes in after RA
GAME, a sport, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Street children play games among the travelling fairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts children at the fair; 'in' is the instruction to place one piece inside another, not a location.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean ragged, scruffy street children.

clue.text: What's found in first-aid kit? In part, swab and a gel

indicators.note: 'in part' means partly, so only part of the phrase that follows is used

blocks.note: swaB AND A GEl

explanation.surface: Inventory of a first-aid kit: swabs and gel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lists first-aid items, so a solver hunts for synonyms of swab and gel; the answer is another first-aid item sitting among them.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a strip of cloth for wrapping wounds is a staple of any medical kit.

clue.text: I and others are ... or used to be ...?

definitions.note: the first definition is the full phrase 'we are', written as a contraction; the apostrophe is ignored

blocks.note: I and others = we; add 'are' and contract the two words
the past tense of 'are'

explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords ignore apostrophes, so WE'RE and WERE fill the grid the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: The contraction of 'we are', and the past form of 'are' as in 'we used to be'.

clue.text: Lays open the topics

blocks.note: exposes someone to something, as to criticism
matters under discussion

explanation.surface: Someone opens up the matters under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: SUBJECTS is a verb in one sense (stress on the second syllable) and a noun in the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb meaning to expose someone to something, and a noun for the matters discussed.

clue.text: Somewhat nastier, overprivileging bluer blood in élitist reactions, primarily?

definitions.text: Somewhat nastier, overprivileging bluer blood in élitist reactions, primarily?

indicators.note: 'primarily' means first of all, so take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Somewhat nastier, overprivileging bluer blood in élitist reactions
blocks.note: Somewhat Nastier Overprivileging Bluer Blood In Élitist Reactions

explanation.surface: A description of people who favour aristocrats in a sneering, élitist way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the recipe and a fair description of the answer; the accent on É is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes being more of a snob: favouring blue blood and élitist attitudes.

clue.text: Removes crusted matter from stinking sled case

indicators.note: stinking means rotten or bad, so the letters are in a bad state

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone cleans the crust off a smelly sledge cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like cleaning a sled; the crust is limescale, as in a kettle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: taking off limescale, the hard crust in kettles and pipes.

clue.text: Reportedly deserves coffee in large quantities, here

definitions.note: the definition is a description of where coffee is held, standing for the noun URNS

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: to deserve is to earn; in British speech, with no R sounded, the two words match

explanation.surface: Someone has earned plenty of coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: Urns are large metal containers for making and serving tea or coffee in bulk, as at a church hall or canteen.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: big vessels with taps are where coffee is kept in bulk.

clue.text: Meal prepared with headless fish for Abraham's son

indicators.note: food that is prepared is worked on, so the letters are reworked
a word without its head has lost its first letter

blocks.note: part of the fodder
FISH without its first letter

explanation.surface: A fish dish is cooked for a biblical figure.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Abraham's first son was born to Hagar.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Bible names two sons of Abraham, this one and Isaac.

clue.text: Golden Gate – first, cake!

indicators.note: 'first' puts the word before it at the front, ahead of the gold

blocks.note: taken as it stands
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: An excited cry about San Francisco's Golden Gate and a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden Gate' reads as the bridge; split it and put GATE first.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the French word for cake, used in English for a rich layered cream cake.

clue.text: Circus venue's not quiet: audience finally seeing 'Piggy'

indicators.note: P is the musical symbol for quiet (piano), so 'not quiet' removes a P
'finally' means at the end, so take the last letter of the word

blocks.note: BIG TOP, a circus tent, without P
last letter of audiencE

explanation.surface: A circus audience turns noisy on seeing a performer called Piggy.
explanation.walkthrough: In the children's rhyme 'This little piggy went to market', each piggy is a toe, and the big toe is the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Nursery slang: in 'This little piggy' each toe is a piggy, the largest going to market.

clue.text: Allow granny to hang loose?

blocks.note: not a grandmother but a granny knot, a badly tied reef knot
permit, the start of a request
not telling someone to relax, but letting a tied rope fall free

explanation.surface: Someone tells an older relative to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang loose' is slang for relax, so granny looks like a person; once she is a knot, letting her hang loose means untying her.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: undoing a granny knot lets the rope hang loose.

clue.text: Patient type is fast at work, case bringing professional pride

indicators.note: letters at work are busy moving about into a new order

blocks.note: Job, the biblical figure famous for his patience
the letters of IS FAST rearranged
a case in law is an action, a lawsuit

explanation.surface: A patient, quick worker takes pride in the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient type' looks like someone in hospital; it is Job, whose patience is proverbial.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: the contentment of doing one's work well is a kind of pride in it.

clue.text: Peninsula? Wrong answer

blocks.note: a wrong is a crime
A = answer, as in Q and A

explanation.surface: A quiz: asked for a peninsula, someone gives the wrong answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a quizmaster rejecting an answer; 'wrong' is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: it juts into the Black Sea from Ukraine.

clue.text: 'Plaiting twists': some youngsters talk this way

definitions.note: the definition is a description of a way of talking, standing for the noun PIG LATIN

indicators.note: the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Children chat about hair plaits.
explanation.walkthrough: Pig Latin is a children's word game that moves the first sound of each word to the end and adds 'ay'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a play language children use to keep secrets from adults.

clue.text: Star is earnest, did you say?

indicators.note: asks about what was spoken, so go by sound

blocks.note: serious = earnest

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether a celebrity is sincere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' reads as a celebrity; it is the one in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Dog Star is the brightest in the night sky.

clue.text: Without changes, Benedict's regularly failing, in my view

indicators.note: letters fail at regular intervals, so every other one drops out

blocks.note: as is = unchanged
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of bEnEdIcT

explanation.surface: Benedict keeps failing, in the speaker's opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of Benedict's is a link, not a letter: only BENEDICT is thinned out.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a phrase that introduces a personal opinion.
